raw_case_text: A 28-year-old Caucasian woman, human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) seronegative, vaccinated at birth with the Bacillus Calmette-Guerin (BCG) vaccine, without any previous medical history, became pregnant after the fourth IVF attempt. According to the available clinical data, the patient did not have any multisystemic symptoms during the previous IVF attempts. During her childhood, when she was 7 years old, her father was treated for drug-sensitive tuberculosis (DST), and it is still unknown if she was evaluated at the time as a person from the household. The initial chest X-ray done at the time of the pregnancy initiation was without pathological changes (Figure 1). At the end of the third month of pregnancy, the patient started experiencing dry cough, intermittent high fever up to 39 C, abdominal pain, and vaginal bleeding. The pregnancy was terminated at the end of the first trimester by hysterotomy because of extensive vaginal bleeding, and two stillborn fetuses (male and female, weighing 60 and 80 g) were evacuated from the uterus. Methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA) was isolated from the uterine cavity. During the following post-partum period, the patient remained febrile despite the treatment with numerous antibiotics regimens containing carbapenems, vancomycin, and piperacillin-tazobactam. One month after delivery she underwent computerized tomography (CT) of pulmonary artery examination, which revealed scattered reticular and micronodular changes in the pulmonary parenchyma without evidence of pulmonary thromboembolic disease. Three months after delivery, the patient started experiencing nausea, vomiting, and weight loss, and in the next 6 months, she started having strong headaches. The nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) of the brain was performed and showed multiple nodular lesions in the brain parenchyma which were characterized as possible metastatic changes (Figure 2). The patient was finally referred to the tertiary-level hospital institution for further diagnostic evaluation under the suspicion of having a disseminated malignant disease. At the time of hospital admission, the chest X-ray revealed diffuse miliary changes. The CT examination of the chest and upper abdomen revealed diffuse micronodular changes in both lungs (Figure 3). The patient underwent a bronchoscopy examination which showed signs of mild bronchial inflammation. Sputum and tracheobronchial samples were sent for GeneX-pert MTB/RIF assay analysis and came back positive. The antituberculosis treatment was initiated with the standard antituberculosis drug regimen consisting of isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol. To determine the extent of the disease, positron emission tomography (PET) was performed and revealed the enhanced metabolic activity in the brain, lungs, mediastinum, liver, ileocecal, and genitourinary area. The final microbiologic confirmation of tuberculosis infection we got later was in the form of positive Lowenstein-Jenssen cultures of the sputum, tracheobronchial lavage, blood, urine, and menstrual blood. Mycobacterium tuberculosis strain was sensitive to all standard antituberculosis drugs. After the initiation of antituberculosis treatment, the patient experienced a favorable clinical outcome, with the complete resolution of all previously described pathological findings, including the complete resolution of the brain lesions, as was shown on the follow-up NMR of the brain (Figure 4).

subjective.chief_complaint: A 28-year-old HIV-negative Caucasian woman presented with a 9-month postpartum course of persistent fever, nausea, vomiting, weight loss, and severe headaches following a first-trimester pregnancy loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: After conceiving on her fourth IVF attempt (with a normal baseline CXR), the patient developed dry cough, high fevers up to 39 °C, abdominal pain, and severe vaginal bleeding at the end of the third month of gestation, requiring hysterotomy evacuation of twin stillborn fetuses. Postpartum fevers persisted despite broad-spectrum antibiotics (carbapenems, vancomycin, piperacillin-tazobactam) for intrauterine MRSA, followed by micronodular changes on 1-month CTPA, nausea, vomiting, and weight loss at 3 months postpartum, and severe headaches with multiple brain nodules on MRI by 9 months postpartum.
subjective.past_medical_history: BCG-vaccinated at birth; HIV-seronegative; conceived via fourth IVF attempt. Household contact with her father who was treated for drug-susceptible tuberculosis when she was 7 years old.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for dry cough, persistent high fevers, postpartum weight loss, nausea, vomiting, and severe headaches.

objective.routine_investigations: HIV serology negative; baseline pre-IVF CXR was normal, whereas tertiary admission CXR showed diffuse bilateral miliary mottling. Uterine cavity culture at pregnancy termination had grown MRSA.
objective.advanced_workup: One-month postpartum CTPA showed scattered reticular and micronodular lung infiltrates without pulmonary embolism. Brain MRI at 9 months postpartum demonstrated multiple parenchymal nodular lesions initially suspected to be metastases. Tertiary admission chest and upper abdominal CT confirmed diffuse bilateral miliary micronodules. Bronchoscopy showed mild bronchial inflammation. Whole-body FDG-PET demonstrated hypermetabolic activity in the brain, lungs, mediastinum, liver, ileocecal region, and genitourinary tract.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Sputum and tracheobronchial lavage samples tested positive on GeneXpert MTB/RIF, and Lowenstein-Jensen cultures of sputum, tracheobronchial lavage, blood, urine, and menstrual blood all grew pan-susceptible Mycobacterium tuberculosis, confirming IVF-associated disseminated miliary tuberculosis with CNS tuberculomas, hepatic, ileocecal, and genitourinary/endometrial involvement. Standard quadruple anti-tuberculosis therapy (isoniazid, rifampin, pyrazinamide, ethambutol) resulted in complete clinical recovery and full resolution of brain tuberculomas on follow-up brain MRI.
